newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn sticks firm to Buba asset revaluation plan.
newsitem.headline: Bonn sticks firm to Buba asset revaluation plan.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition vowed after a crisis meeting on Germany's budget woes to push ahead with its controversial plan to revalue the Bundesbank's gold and currency reserves.
"On the question of the revaluation, we are still unified in the belief that this is right," Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl told journalists outside Kohl's office early on Monday.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who avoided the press after the four-hour meeting, wants to revalue the Bundesbank's gold and currency assets despite objections from the mighty central bank, which sees the plan as an attack on its fabled independence.

But press commentators and some junior members of the ruling coalition criticised the government's stubborn attitude in the face of the bank's fierce resistance and said the row could tear apart the coalition and cause turmoil across Europe.
Bohl said the coalition was still at odds over plans to fill gaps in the budget, which are threatening Germany's bid to qualify for the European Union's planned single currency.
But he reiterated its commitment to the timetable and entry criteria for European monetary union (EMU).

Bohl revealed an added dimension to the government's troubles, pointing out there could still be problems balancing the 1997 budget even if it could raise funds as planned through an accelerated privatisation of assets.

Kohl's coalition partners, the liberal Free Democrats (FDP), have adamantly said they will not approve tax increases to plug holes in the budget, suggesting that the future of the coalition could be at stake if Waigel insists on tax rises.
Waigel, who has to cope with a 15 billion mark tax shortfall this year and higher-than-forecast spending because of high unemployment, has said taxes increases cannot be ruled out.
His plan to reap 20 billion marks from the revaluation of Bundesbank assets could party ease the government's debt burden and help Germany to meet the single currency entry criteria.

Bohl said Waigel would state the government's position on the plan in a special debate in parliament on Wednesday and would also discuss the legal text for the proposed bill on revaluation with the Bundesbank.
Hans Tietmeyer, the head of the Bundesbank, denied a report in Der Spiegel magazine that he had proposed a delay in the 1999 start date for Europe's single currency.

He insisted he was committed to the European Union's Maastricht Treaty, but reiterated the Bundesbank's opposition to the revaluing its reserves and called on Bonn to take proper note of its objections.
Spiegel had quoted Tietmeyer as breaking one of Kohl's political taboos by asking if Bonn and Paris could delay the start of the single currency.

Some members of Kohl's coalition also voiced opposition to Waigel's revaluation plan, raising the possibility that the veteran chancellor might not be able to muster a majority to push the controversial measure through parliament.
FDP budget expert Juergen Koppelin urged the government to retreat from what was shaping up to be an unprecedented clash with the central bank.
Juergen Augustinowitz, a young Christian Democrat who has already announced he will not vote for legislation opposed by the Bundesbank, said he was sure he would not be alone.
Several dailies said Kohl could no longer be sure of his slim 12-seat parliamentary majority.

The conservative Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung newspaper said Kohl's coalition had manoeuvered itself into "a most unenviable" position by taking on the Bundesbank and said it was now fighting a "growing sense of despair."

"Waigel's financial policies have made it difficult for Germany to qualify for EMU and have damaged Germany's ambitions to lead the march into the currency union," it said. "The government can try to counter the will of the Bundesbank, but it may not be able to count on its slim majority holding up."
